native_result.query: How does incarceration affect the wealth of black individuals based on their income levels?
native_result.HypoA: The negative impact of incarceration on wealth for black individuals may be less for the high-income group than those at lower wealth ranges.
native_result.HypoB:
## Final Hypothesis (data-grounded)

Among Black respondents in the NLS79 (n = 3,013), having been jailed at any point between 1985 and 1994 is associated with substantially lower wealth in 1996 across every pre-period wealth/SES tier, but the pattern is not monotonic and corresponds to neither candidate hypothesis cleanly. At the headline level, ever-jailed Black respondents have 1996 median wealth of $0 (vs $5,000 for never-jailed), a 57.2% share at exactly $0 wealth (vs 32.9% for never-jailed), and a flat median Δ(1996 − 1985) wealth of $0 with a winsorized-1% mean Δ of $4,576, while never-jailed peers grow by a median $2,200 (winsorized-1% mean Δ = $33,578). A logistic regression of P(wealth_1996 = 0) on ever_jailed, sex, and pre-period 1985 wealth quartile yields an adjusted odds ratio for ever_jailed of 2.52 (95% CI 1.78 – 3.57, p < 0.001), and a sex-adjusted OLS of Δ wealth on ever_jailed with the same covariates plus log1p(1985 wealth) yields a coefficient of −$37,146 (p = 0.006, 95% CI [−$63,549, −$10,743]). Tier-by-tier the picture is mixed: in Q1 (lowest pre-period 1985 wealth; 76 jailed vs 1,240 never) both groups are pinned at a $0 median in 1996 and the ever-jailed are only +17.0 pp more likely to be at $0 (65.8% vs 48.8%); in Q2 (only 7 jailed — too thin to be informative) the gap is modest in level (median 1996 $2,000 vs $5,000, MW p = 0.41 / 0.54); in Q3 (42 vs 715) the ever-jailed drop to $0 while never-jailed are at $12,000, a +45.4 pp share-at-zero gap and a $10,700 median Δ gap; in Q4 (top pre-period tier, 34 vs 714) the ever-jailed lose $8,000 of wealth on the median while never-jailed gain $6,888, a $14,888 absolute swing — the largest gap in the table — and Mann-Whitney is significant (p = 0.008 on Δ, p = 0.0008 on 1996 level). Tertiles reproduce the same direction in every band (T1, T2, T3) and the male-only sensitivity (dropping the 16 jailed Black females) is essentially identical. Read against the two candidate hypotheses, the data rejects H1 — the deficit does not shrink in the top tier; it is in fact largest there in absolute dollars — and only partially supports H2 — the ever-jailed are stuck at the floor in Q1 and Q3, but not in Q2 or Q4, and the absolute $-gap is not constant; the cleanest summary is the adjusted OR of 2.52 for zero wealth and the ~$37k adjusted Δ shortfall, which together describe a wealth-trajectory collapse across pre-period wealth tiers within the Black subsample that contradicts H1 and only partly matches H2. Caveats carried into the conclusion (and not corrected away): pre-period 1985 wealth medians are already lower for the ever-jailed ($320 vs $764) so the comparison has selection on prior wealth, the ever_jailed window (1985–1994) overlaps with the 1985 wealth measurement so jail exposure is partly contemporaneous with the baseline, and ever_jailed is treated as observational throughout.

sub_hypo.text: The incarceration-associated wealth disadvantage varies nonmonotonically across baseline wealth quartiles: the lowest tier shares a zero median, while the second tier has a modest and imprecisely estimated wealth-level gap.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLS79 respondents in Q1 and Q2 of pre-period 1985 wealth; Q1 includes 76 ever-jailed and 1,240 never-jailed respondents, and Q2 includes only 7 ever-jailed respondents.

sub_hypo.text: Black respondents jailed during 1985–1994 exhibit substantial wealth disadvantages in the third and highest baseline wealth quartiles, with the largest absolute wealth-change gap in the highest quartile.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLS79 respondents in Q3 and Q4 of pre-period 1985 wealth; Q3 includes 42 ever-jailed and 715 never-jailed respondents, and Q4 includes 34 and 714, respectively.
sub_hypo.relations: In Q3, median 1996 wealth is $0 for ever-jailed versus $12,000 for never-jailed, the ever-jailed zero-wealth share is 45.4 percentage points higher, and the median wealth-change gap is $10,700. In Q4, median wealth change is −$8,000 versus +$6,888, a $14,888 absolute gap, the largest reported tier gap. Q4 Mann–Whitney tests are significant for wealth change (p = 0.008) and 1996 wealth level (p = 0.0008).

sub_hypo.text: The tier-specific pattern contradicts a deficit that shrinks in the top tier and only partially supports a common zero-wealth floor or constant absolute dollar gap.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLS79 respondents compared across pre-period 1985 wealth quartiles.
sub_hypo.relations: The pattern is nonmonotonic. H1 is rejected because the absolute-dollar deficit is largest rather than smaller in the top tier. H2 receives only partial support because ever-jailed median wealth is at the zero floor in Q1 and Q3 but not Q2 or Q4, and absolute dollar gaps are not constant.

sub_hypo.text: The direction of the incarceration-associated wealth disadvantage persists across baseline wealth tertiles and in a male-only sensitivity analysis.
sub_hypo.context: Black NLS79 respondents grouped into 1985 wealth tertiles T1–T3; a separate male-only sensitivity analysis excludes 16 ever-jailed Black females.
sub_hypo.relations: Tertile analyses reproduce the same direction of disadvantage in every band, and the male-only results are essentially identical.
